headline: Mining Giant Honored for 30 Years of Pit Lake Restoration
meta_description: BHP wins BC reclamation award for three decades of environmental work at former Island Copper Mine, using innovative lake treatment to neutralize acid drainage.
summary_short: BHP receives honor for 30 years of monitoring and restoration at closed Island Copper Mine near Port Hardy, transforming a 1,320-foot pit into a managed ecosystem.
body:
When the Island Copper Mine near Port Hardy, British Columbia, exhausted its orebody in 1995 after 24 years of operation, it left behind a wound in the landscape: a pit spiraling 1,320 feet into the Earth. Rather than abandon the site, BHP—the world's largest mining company—committed to a restoration project that would span three decades. This year, the BC Technical Research Committee on Reclamation recognized that commitment with its Annual Reclamation Award, honoring a approach to environmental stewardship that transforms industrial scars into stable ecosystems.

The solution was innovative: BHP flooded the pit with seawater to create a stratified lake, then injected acid rock drainage—a toxic byproduct of mineral oxidation—into oxygen-depleted bottom waters where it could be neutralized. Since 2001, the company has refined the system by fertilizing surface waters every 7 to 10 days, stimulating plankton blooms that absorb contaminant heavy metals before sinking. The work extends far beyond chemistry. Remote monitoring systems reduce worker safety risks, while improved infrastructure provides resilience against extreme weather and power failures.

The Island Copper Mine once employed 900 people and transformed Port Hardy from a small settlement into a town of 5,000. When closure came, that commitment to community and environment didn't end—it transformed. The TRCR noted that BHP's ongoing adaptive management has "strengthened environmental protection" and "enhanced long-term reliability" of the treatment system. This award reflects a larger truth about modern mining: the real measure of an operation isn't just what it extracts, but what it leaves behind, and how seriously a company tends to that legacy long after the pickaxes are hung up.
quick_facts: Island Copper Mine pit descended 1,320 feet underground, deepest point touched by sun on Earth
BHP employed 900 workers at peak; mine operated 1971 to 1995 near Port Hardy, BC
Pit Lake treatment system uses plankton blooms to absorb heavy metals every 7–10 days
30 years of continuous monitoring and reclamation work wins 2024 BC award
